2.title: Why is traditional sleep medicine facing a clinical bottleneck?
detailed: Why is traditional sleep medicine facing a clinical bottleneck?
Look at the cycle between the Patient, the Physician and the Hospital.
First, Fragmented Data: it provides limited, single-night snapshot data.
Second, Hospital Reliance: it demands extensive medical resources and physical bed space.
Third, Patient Inconvenience: it requires patients to visit hospitals specifically for data collection.
And Treatment Blindspots: it is difficult to track if interventions are actually executed or effective at home.

Fragmented Data, Hospital Reliance, Patient Inconvenience, and Treatment Blindspots.

6.title: Radar principle diagram
detailed: Here is how the radar works.
The Radar sits at a distance, D0, from the User.
It sends a signal from Tx and picks up the reflection at Rx.
A small chest movement, Δx, changes the received pulse.
We see this as the time of flight, ToF, and the phase shift, Δφ.
From these changes we rebuild the breathing, with no wires.

8.title: A Three-Phase Technical Roadmap
detailed: A Three-Phase Technical Roadmap Validates Radar from Sleep Lab to Cardiology.
Core Technology Base: 24-GHz Continuous-Wave Radar combined with Deep Neural Decision Trees.
Phase 1: Clinical Purity (N=196). Mapped directly against gold-standard Polysomnography (PSG). Strong correlation (r=0.91).
Phase 2: Real-World Utility (80 patients, 147 nights). Demonstrated home sleep assessment without the need for professional intervention or setup.
Phase 3: Cross-Domain Translation (N=72). Radar-captured Periodic Breathing (PB) was associated with Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF) impairment.

Phase 3: Cross-Domain Translation (N=72): Periodic Breathing was associated with LVEF impairment.

11.title: Airflow Defines the Event; Radar Sees the Chest Wall
detailed: Airflow Defines the Event; Radar Sees the Chest Wall.
Standard scoring and radar look at two different signals.
Standard scoring: airflow. After normal breathing, airflow stops (apnea) or becomes shallow (hypopnea).
These events are visible only when airflow itself is measured.
Radar: chest-wall motion. Radar senses the rise and fall of the chest wall, not airflow.
This creates blind spots when chest motion is read as if it were airflow.
Blind spot: in obstructive events, breathing effort continues while airflow is absent, so chest motion alone does not equal airflow.
Radar must therefore recognise a characteristic sequence of chest-motion changes.

12.title: The Radar-Detectable Sleep-Breathing Event
detailed: The Radar-Detectable Sleep-Breathing Event: a characteristic five-phase sequence of chest-wall motion.
1, Normal breathing: regular chest excursion at normal amplitude.
2, Apnea onset: amplitude drops markedly or stops completely.
3, Struggling effort: airway still closed: small up-and-down movements from effort to breathe.
4, Recovery surge: airway opens: one large excursion as breathing recovers.
5, Back to normal: amplitude returns to the normal level.
This full sequence of chest-wall changes is the sleep-breathing event that radar can detect.
concise: Normal breathing, Apnea onset, Struggling effort, Recovery surge, Back to normal.

15.title: From Validation to the Ward: A Zero-Contact Care Platform
detailed: From Validation to the Ward: A Zero-Contact Care Platform. The radar platform in routine inpatient use.
Sleep-Breathing Health Care Platform: Breathing: continuous, contact-free respiratory monitoring. Heart rate: tracked from the same radar signal. Bed status: in-bed / out-of-bed and movement status.
Alerts sent to the care team: Prolonged bed exit: alert reminder when a patient is out of bed too long.
Abnormal vital-sign values: flagged on the ward dashboard. Push notifications: Dashboard and LINE Notify messages to staff.
National quality recognition: 2021 SNQ, Symbol of National Quality; 2022 NHQA, Distinctive Center – Sleep Center.

38.title: Take-Home Messages
detailed: 1. Technological Leap: 24-GHz contactless radar provides continuous, multi-night monitoring without patient friction.
2. Proven Stability: Agreement maintained across both highly controlled hospital settings (r=0.91) and unmanaged daily home environments (r=0.87).
3. Validated Screening: Functions as a sensitive (90.5%) TFDA-cleared screen for suspected severe OSA (bRDI ≥ 30).
4. Expanding Horizons: Ongoing research demonstrates potential for cross-domain monitoring, identifying associations between periodic breathing and cardiac impairment.
5. Real-World Recognition: SNQ (2021) and NHQA (2022, 2025) national quality awards.
